identity_notes: Maca (Lepidium meyenii) human RCT evidence clusters mainly around sexual function/libido (modest positive effects independent of sex hormone levels), menopausal symptom relief (a coherent positive series of 'Maca-GO' trials from one research group, though with a distinctive placebo effect noted repeatedly), and antidepressant-induced sexual dysfunction; systematic reviews consistently caveat that trial numbers, sample sizes, and methodological quality are too limited for firm conclusions. The single most important applicability caveat: maca is sold in multiple distinct color/type variants (yellow, black, red, gelatinized 'Maca-GO') with DIFFERENT reported effect profiles in the same reviewed literature (e.g., black maca improves sperm production while red maca does not; red maca showed better mood/energy effects than black maca in a head-to-head trial), so 'maca' is not interchangeable across products, and label_material_match is often unclear/related_form_differs rather than exact_match. Semen-quality evidence is itself contradictory across time: an earlier systematic review (27621241, 2016) reported suggestive positive effects, while a more recent meta-analysis (36110519, 2022) found no significant pooled effect on sperm concentration. Safety signals include a testosterone-immunoassay interference artifact, a case of probable lead contamination in a commercial maca powder product, and a case report of hepatotoxicity from a maca 'medicinal liquor' preparation.
